extracted.intended_audience: graduate students (or advanced undergraduates) learning algebraic geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, examples, and exercises about scheme-valued/field-valued/ring-valued points, maps to projective schemes, maps of graded rings and Proj, rational maps and birationality, representable functors, and group schemes from a textbook chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Z-valued and A-valued points (functor of points)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Z is a scheme, the Z-valued points of a scheme X, denoted X(Z), are maps Z → X. If A is a ring, the A-valued points of X, denoted X(A), are defined to be the (Spec A)-valued points of X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the functor-of-points viewpoint: X can be viewed as the contravariant functor h_X from schemes to sets X ↦ Mor(–, X). When working over a base scheme B, the structure maps Z → B (or Spec A → B) are implicitly part of the data. Warning: a k-valued point of a k-scheme is sometimes called a 'rational point' (dangerous terminology); prefer 'k-valued point'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of A-valued points for affine schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: For an affine scheme Spec Z[x1, …, xn]/(f1, …, fr), the A-valued points are precisely the solutions in the ring A to f1(x1,…,xn)=…=fr(x1,…,xn)=0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rational solutions to x^2+y^2=16 are Q-valued points of Spec Z[x,y]/(x^2+y^2−16); integral solutions are Z-valued points. For A local, A-valued points of a general scheme admit a good interpretation; Z-valued points of projective space can be subtle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology caution: 'Z-valued point' vs scheme point
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'Z-valued point' (or 'A-valued point') does not necessarily mean a point of the underlying topological space of a scheme; it's a map from Z (or Spec A) to X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The terminology is unfortunate and inconsistent in the literature; consult index under 'point' for examples of inconsistent modifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphisms induce maps on Z-valued points
rubrics_metrics.description: A morphism of schemes X → Y induces, for any scheme Z, a map of sets X(Z) → Y(Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise (easy): show X → Y induces X(Z) → Y(Z). Conversely, morphisms are not determined by their underlying maps of topological points, but they are determined by their induced maps on Z-valued points as Z varies over all schemes (Hint: take Z = X; this amounts to Yoneda's Lemma).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functor-of-points viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: The notation X(Z) suggests interpreting X as the contravariant functor h_X : Sch → Sets sending Z ↦ Mor(Z, X).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This viewpoint makes A-valued points a natural and powerful language; it motivates representable functors, Yoneda's Lemma, and many concrete descriptions (e.g., affine-scheme solutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps to projective space from n+1 functions with no common zeros
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a B-scheme and f0,…,fn are n+1 functions on X with no common zeros, then [f0:…:fn] gives a morphism of B-schemes X → P^n_B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If g is nowhere vanishing on X, then [f0:…:fn] and [g f0: … : g fn] define the same morphism. This construction explains many explicit maps to projective space but not all: global functions may be insufficient, and sections of line bundles are needed for the general characterization (see Theorem 16.4.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all maps to projective schemes arise from global functions
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist morphisms to projective schemes that cannot be written using global functions f0,…,fn on the source; one must allow sections of line bundles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the identity map P^1 → P^1 cannot be produced from global (nonconstant) functions because P^1 has no nonconstant global functions. Theorem 16.4.1 gives the correct generalization using line-bundle sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization with nilpotents: Spec C[ε]/(ε^2) as tangent vector
rubrics_metrics.description: Spec C[ε]/(ε^2) can be pictured as a point with an attached tangent vector, and maps from it to a scheme encode tangential (infinitesimal) information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises invite thinking how maps behave when nilpotents are present and how pictures change if parameters vanish; see Exercise 12.1.I for extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps of graded rings inducing morphisms of Proj
rubrics_metrics.description: A graded ring map φ : S → R (preserving grading up to a fixed d>0, i.e., Sn → R_{dn}) can induce a morphism Proj R  ackslash V(φ(S+)) → Proj S; if V(φ(S+)) = ∅ then there is a morphism Proj R → Proj S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: for each homogeneous f ∈ S+ define maps on distinguished opens D(φ(f)) and glue. If φ is a map of A-algebras, the induced map is a morphism of A-schemes. See (6.4.0.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic criterion for V(φ(S+)) = ∅
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ(S+) generates the irrelevant ideal (i.e., (φ(S+)) = R+), then V(φ(S+)) = ∅ and the hypothesis for an induced Proj morphism is satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 6.4.B suggests using algebraic checks (e.g., Exercise 4.5.I) can be easier than geometric verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-uniqueness: different graded-ring maps can give same scheme morphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Different maps of graded rings may yield the same morphism between the associated Proj schemes; constructions are insensitive to what happens in finitely many degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 6.4.C exhibits rings where different graded maps induce the same Proj isomorphism. Later exercises (Veronese subrings, regrading) explain ways to remedy or understand this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Veronese subring and regrading
rubrics_metrics.description: For a graded ring S = ⊕_n S_n, the nth Veronese subring S^{(n)} = ⊕_j S_{nj} is a regrading that can make a finitely generated graded ring generated in (new) degree 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 6.4.D–6.4.G show how Veronese subrings and choosing suitable d allow assuming finitely generated graded rings are generated in degree 1 after regrading, which helps embed Proj in projective space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rational map definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational map π : X ⇢ Y is an equivalence class of pairs (α: U → Y) where U is a dense open subset of X and α is a morphism; two representatives (α: U→Y) and (β: V→Y) are equivalent if they agree on a dense open subset of U∩V.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rational map need not be a morphism (hence the careful notation). For S-schemes one requires the representatives to be S-morphisms. There's a generalization for nonreduced X called pseudo-morphisms, but rational maps from reduced schemes to separated schemes behave particularly well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant rational maps
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational map π : X ⇢ Y is dominant if for some (hence every) representative U → Y the image is dense in Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For irreducible schemes, π is dominant iff it sends the generic point of X to the generic point of Y (Exercise 6.5.A). A morphism that is a dominant rational map is called a dominant morphism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and category of dominant rational maps
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominant rational maps between integral schemes compose (in a well-defined way), and if X is irreducible, composing a dominant π:X⇢Y with ρ:Y⇢Z gives a dominant ρ∘π if ρ is dominant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integral schemes with dominant rational maps form an interesting category; in classical situations this corresponds to inclusions of function fields in the opposite direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between rational maps and function field inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: In suitable classical situations (integral finite type k-schemes), dominant rational maps correspond to inclusions of function fields in the opposite direction; conversely an inclusion K(Y) ↪ K(X) preserving k induces a dominant rational map X ⇢ Y (Proposition 6.5.7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: not every map of function fields gives a rational map of schemes in all contexts (example: Spec k[x] vs Spec k(x) have same function field but no corresponding rational map of k-schemes). Proposition 6.5.7 constructs maps by replacing Y with an affine open and localizing appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birational maps and birationality
rubrics_metrics.description: A rational map π : X ⇢ Y is birational if it is dominant and there exists a dominant rational inverse ψ such that π∘ψ and ψ∘π are the identity in the equivalence class (i.e., identity on some dense open).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Birationality is the notion of isomorphism in the category of integral schemes with dominant rational maps. A birational morphism may have only a rational inverse. For reduced schemes, X and Y are birational iff they contain dense open subschemes U≅V (Proposition 6.5.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of integral affine variety with specified function field
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a finitely generated field extension K/k, there exists an irreducible affine k-variety whose function field is K (Exercise 6.5.C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction via taking a surjection k[t1,…,tn] → k[x1,…,xn] mapping ti ↦ xi and letting the kernel be a prime ideal p; then Spec(k[t1,…,tn]/p) has fraction field K. Geometrically, take closure of the image of Spec K → Spec k[t1,…,tn].

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of categories: integral varieties and function fields
rubrics_metrics.description: There are equivalences among: (a) category of integral k-varieties with dominant rational maps; (b) integral affine k-varieties with dominant rational maps; (c) opposite category of finitely generated field extensions of k with inclusions extending id_k (Exercise 6.5.D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus birationality/rationality questions can be translated into algebraic questions about function fields; an integral affine k-variety is rational iff its function field is purely transcendental over k.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical examples: parametrization of conics and Pythagorean triples
rubrics_metrics.description: The circle x^2+y^2=1 has a birational map with A^1 given by projecting from a rational point; rational slopes m give explicit rational parametrization x=(m^2−1)/(m^2+1), y=−2m/(m^2+1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a birational map C ⇢ P^1 and can be extended over points in some cases (foreshadowing the Curve-to-Projective Extension Theorem 16.5.1). Exercises ask to use this to generate all Pythagorean triples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension over regular codimension 1 points (foreshadow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Domains of definition of rational maps to projective schemes often extend over regular codimension 1 points; this will be made precise in the Curve-to-Projective Extension Theorem 16.5.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and exercises (e.g., Cremona transformation, conics) illustrate extension phenomena and limitations when codimension one sets are singular or nonregular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cremona transformation example
rubrics_metrics.description: The classical Cremona rational map P^2 ⇢ P^2 given by [x:y:z] ↦ [1/x:1/y:1/z] has domain of definition larger than the locus xyz ≠ 0 and can be extended over some codimension 1 sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise explores the domain of definition and shows extension beyond naive loci, again illustrating extension over codimension 1 sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps to A^1 correspond to global functions
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural bijection Mor(X, A^1_Z) ↔ Γ(X, O_X) for any scheme X (maps to A^1 correspond to global sections of the structure sheaf).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This bijection is functorial in X and restated as an instance of representability: the global-section functor is represented by A^1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representable functors and representability definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a category C and an object Y in C, the contravariant functor h_Y : C → Sets defined by h_Y(X)=Mor(X,Y) represents objects mapping to Y. A contravariant functor F is representable if F ≅ h_Y for some Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bijection Mor(X,A^1) ↔ Γ(X,O_X) says the global-section functor is representable by A^1. Representing objects (when they exist) are unique up to unique isomorphism (Exercise 6.6.C; a universal-property argument).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of representable functors: A^n and G_m
rubrics_metrics.description: Affine n-space A^n represents the functor sending X to n-tuples of global functions (Γ(X,O_X))^n. The functor sending X to invertible functions Γ(X,O_X)^× is represented by Spec Z[t,t^{-1}] = G_m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 6.6.E guides these verifications. G_m over a field k is Spec k[t,t^{-1}] and represents the multiplicative group of invertible functions in k-schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spec A represents maps of locally ringed spaces to A
rubrics_metrics.description: For a ring A (or scheme Z), the functor sending a locally ringed space X to Hom(Spec A, X) (or to maps induced by A) is representable by Spec A (Exercise 6.6.F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This motivates the definition of Spec A: it represents the functor of maps from schemes to the affine scheme associated to A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group object (group scheme) axioms in a category
rubrics_metrics.description: A group object in a category C with final object Z and products is an object X together with morphisms m: X×X → X (multiplication), i: X → X (inverse), e: Z → X (identity) satisfying the usual group axioms (associativity, identity, inverse) expressed as commutative diagrams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the category of schemes, such an X is called a group scheme. Example: A^1 has group-like structures induced by addition; G_m is the multiplicative group scheme. The text begins stating the associativity axiom diagram; other axioms follow similarly.
